findings.title: Keyword whitelist lets real passphrase-style secrets through
findings.detail: onlyNames() treats a quoted value as "just a name, not a secret" whenever it is letters-only, camelCase or -/_/.-joined, AND contains one of the substrings ["secret","token","password","passwd","key","client","vault","entry","access","name","id"] anywhere in it (via lower.contains($0), not a word-boundary match). This is meant to let through things like `clientSecret = "clientSecret"`, but it equally lets through a real, low-entropy password/passphrase a developer actually committed, e.g. `password = "my-secret-password"` or `apiKey = "production-access-key"` — both are >=12 chars, contain no digits, are dash-joined lowercase words, and contain "secret"/"password"/"access"/"key", so breaks() returns false and the finding is suppressed. The description explicitly promises "a passphrase … still counts"; the test suite only exercises correct-horse-battery-staple, which was deliberately chosen to avoid every keyword in the list, so the regression isn't caught. Because several keywords ("id", "key", "name") are short, common English substrings, this also triggers on many ordinary dictionary words used in passphrases (e.g. "rapid", "guide", "inside" contain "id"), broadening the bypass well beyond the intended "name for a secret" case and weakening the secret scanner's actual purpose.

findings.title: Special-case dispatch keyed on a literal rule name string
findings.detail: breaks() special-cases the "password or secret" rule purely by comparing rule.name to a hard-coded string literal. If that rule's name is ever changed (e.g. renamed for the Finding it produces), this comparison silently fails and the function falls back to the plain text.contains(rule.pattern) path with no onlyNames filtering at all — re-introducing the original false-positive problem this change fixes, without any compiler or test error pointing at the cause, since rules is a plain [(name:, pattern:)] array rather than an enum or typed case the compiler could check exhaustively.
